title: A three-page paper from 1963 upended the definition of knowledge
body: A long-held view treats knowledge as justified true belief. Edmund Gettier’s tiny paper described cases where all three conditions hold, yet the person was only lucky. Bertrand Russell had a similar example: you glance at a clock that stopped exactly twelve hours ago and believe the right time. Around AD 770, the Indian Buddhist philosopher Dharmottara imagined a traveler who sees a mirage and finds real water there.

slides.question: When did Bertrand Russell publish his stopped-clock example?
slides.explanation: Russell’s stopped clock appears in Human Knowledge: Its Scope and Limits (1948), only 15 years before Gettier’s 1963 paper; Dharmottara’s mirage case dates from around AD 770.

slides.question: Russell’s clock stopped exactly twelve hours ago. Why does that matter for knowledge?
options: You get the right time only by luck
You cannot read a stopped clock
Twelve hours is too long to wait
slides.explanation: Your belief is justified and true, yet right only by luck. Gettier cases like this suggest justified true belief is not enough for knowledge.

slides.heading: Match the thinker to the example
slides.explanation: In each case the belief is justified and true, yet right only by luck.
